summary: Researchers at Nanyang Technological University, led by Hongjin Fan, designed hetero-polyionic hydrogel electrolytes for aqueous rechargeable zinc iodine batteries as a safer alternative to lithium-ion batteries. The hydrogel promotes uniform zinc deposition, immobilizes polyiodides at the cathode and blocks dendrites, giving very stable cycling over 18,000 cycles. Energy density remains far below commercial lithium-ion, and issues of conductivity, compatibility, scalable production and safety must still be solved.
one_line: NTU researchers use charged hetero-hydrogel electrolytes to make aqueous zinc iodine batteries dendrite-free and stable over 18,000 cycles, though energy density still lags lithium-ion.
key_facts: Statista estimated that lithium-ion batteries accounted for 185 GWh of energy consumed in 2020, projected to reach 2,035 GWh by 2030.
Lithium-ion batteries carry a risk of burning or explosion from thermal runaway.
Rechargeable zinc iodine batteries are safer, cheaper and more environmentally friendly than lithium alternatives, but have lower energy output than commercial non-aqueous lithium batteries.
Zinc iodine batteries suffer from zinc dendrite growth and corrosion of the zinc anode, which reduce efficiency and can cause short-circuiting.
Hongjin Fan of Nanyang Technological University's School of Physical and Mathematical Sciences and co-authors published the work in the journal Advanced Materials.
The team designed hydrogel electrolytes with functional groups carrying positive or negative charges, forming a hetero-hydrogel that makes the anode side zincophilic and the cathode side iodophilic.
On the anode side the hydrogel repels dissolved polyiodides, allowing uniform zinc deposition and protecting against iodine-caused corrosion.
At the cathode side polyiodides are immobilized and iodine redox reactions are sped up by synchronized rapid transport of ions and electrons.
The solid hydrogel's mechanical strength acts as a physical barrier limiting dendrite growth, unlike liquid electrolytes.
The test battery showed an ultralow decay rate, retaining its energy storage capacity over 18,000 discharge and recharge cycles, outstripping current zinc iodine batteries.
The adhesion between polyanionic and polycationic hydrogel components is robust enough to limit swelling even without a cellulose paper scaffold.
Fan said the zinc iodine battery's mass and volume energy density is still far from commercial lithium-ion batteries.
Remaining challenges include improving hydrogel ion conductivity and stability, compatibility with electrodes and separators, and large-scale cost-effective production.
Fan stressed rigorous testing of safety, reliability and environmental impact of hydrogel electrolytes from raw material extraction to disposal.
